sentences.text: The skull of Dentaneosuchus was altirostral, meaning it was higher than it was wide.
The premaxilla, a bone at the very front of the snout, contained five teeth on each side.
Notably, the fourth premaxillary tooth was twice the size of the second tooth.
The maxilla and nasal bone were fused together in this animal.
The nasal bone was long and stretched from the front of the rostrum all the way to the frontal bone.
Four osteoderms, which are bony deposits in the skin that form armor, have been discovered, but their exact location on the body is uncertain because no sebecid preserves articulated armor.
These osteoderms included a larger sub-trapezoid type and a smaller ovoid type that was longer than it was wide.
The osteoderms of Dentaneosuchus resemble those of Baurusuchus but are sufficiently distinct to be different.
Dentaneosuchus was the largest terrestrial carnivore of Cenozoic Europe.
The animal exhibited massive size, matching the increase in size seen in contemporary European mammal species.
It could likely prey on animals its own size or larger, such as the early perissodactyl Lophiodon lautricense, which weighed up to 2,000 kg.
The genus Dentaneosuchus was described by Martin and colleagues in 2023.
The type species of Dentaneosuchus is Atacisaurus crassiproratus.
The first fossil of Dentaneosuchus was discovered in the Sables du Castrais Formation near Issel, France, and originally named Atacisaurus crassiproratus by Gaston Astre in 1931.
In 2018, Godinot and colleagues reclassified the species as Iberosuchus crassiproratus.
The type species of the genus Dentaneosuchus is Dentaneosuchus crassiproratus.
There are two recorded fossil occurrences of Dentaneosuchus.
Dentaneosuchus was an apex predator capable of hunting large prey like Lophiodon.
Although the precise prey of Dentaneosuchus is unknown, its great size indicates it was an apex predator in its environment.
The presence of sebecids in Europe, far from their primary range in South America, remains not entirely resolved.
Dentaneosuchus was tentatively recovered as the most basal member of the family Sebecidae.
Phylogenetic analysis places Dentaneosuchus in the family Sebecidae, closely related to the South American Baurusuchidae within the group Sebecosuchia.
Within Sebecidae, Dentaneosuchus was recovered as having affinities with the German genus Bergisuchus.
Dentaneosuchus belongs to the parent group Sebecoidea.
Dentaneosuchus is classified in the class Reptilia.
Dentaneosuchus lived during the Middle Eocene.
The range of Dentaneosuchus is currently confined to the Bartonian stage of the Eocene.
Dentaneosuchus lived from the Ypresian to the Bartonian, between 56 and 37.71 million years ago.
Dentaneosuchus fossils have been found in Issel and Réalmont in France.

Some localities previously associated with Dentaneosuchus were placed in the MP13-14 biozones (Lutetian), an age similar to the Spanish Duero Basin and much older than the Réalmont locality in France.
It is debated why crocodylomorphs lost their position as top predators in Europe by the end of the Eocene.
Researchers suggest that differences between Dentaneosuchus and Bergisuchus might change with age, but conclude it is premature to make conclusive statements on the implications.
Authors note that many unknowns regarding Dentaneosuchus anatomy could greatly impact its phylogenetic placement and that future discoveries could change its position drastically.
The origins of European sebecids are a debated subject due to a poor fossil record outside of South America.
A major issue with the North American dispersal hypothesis is the complete absence of sebecid material in continental North America, with only a ziphodont tooth from Cuba as potential evidence.
